cards.title: Three engines: cardio, strength, flexibility
cards.body: Cardio trains heart and lungs (running, cycling, brisk walking). Strength trains muscles (bodyweight, bands, weights). Flexibility keeps joints moving well (stretching, yoga). A complete routine touches all three.

cards.title: Progressive overload in one breath
cards.body: Do slightly more over time — one more rep, a little more weight, a minute longer. That's the entire secret of getting fitter. The body adapts to stress, so the stress must grow a little to keep adapting.
The couch-to-walk-jog logic: alternate 1 minute jogging with 2 minutes walking, then shrink the walking parts week by week. Tiny increments compound — nobody starts by running 30 minutes straight.
Consistency beats intensity. Three moderate sessions a week will outrun one heroic monthly workout every time. Show up, keep it doable, let the streak do the work.

choices: Lifting the heaviest weight possible once
Gradually increasing training stress over time
cards.explain: Small, steady increases in reps, weight, or duration — that's what signals the body to adapt and grow stronger.

flashcards.back: Exercise that raises heart rate and trains heart/lung endurance — walking, running, cycling, swimming.
Working muscles against resistance — bodyweight, bands, or weights — to build muscle and bone density.
Gradually increasing training stress (reps, weight, time) so the body keeps adapting.
Range of motion around joints, maintained through stretching and full-movement exercise.

questions.q: Which three pillars make a complete routine?
questions.explain: Heart/lungs, muscles, and joints — train all three and nothing important gets neglected.

choices: Adding a little more stress over time
questions.explain: One more rep, slightly heavier, a minute longer. Gradual beats heroic.
Consistency compounds. The best program is the one you actually keep doing.
Muscles support joints and bones — strength work pays off in posture, balance, and everyday capability.
Start easy, progress gradually. The body adapts — but it needs time and patience, not punishment.

cards.title: Warm up for 5 minutes
cards.body: Easy movement — brisk walking, arm circles, leg swings — raises body temperature and loosens joints before harder work. Cold muscles are grumpy muscles; five minutes prevents most beginner strains.

cards.title: Form first, weight second
cards.body: Learn each movement with light or no weight until it feels natural. Good form with light weight builds strength; bad form with heavy weight builds injuries. Film yourself from the side to check.
The 10% rule: don't increase your weekly training volume by more than about 10%. Ran 20 minutes total this week? Aim for 22 next week, not 40. Enthusiasm is the #1 cause of beginner burnout.
Rest days are training days. Muscles rebuild during rest, not during the workout — schedule 1–2 rest days weekly. And soreness is not a scoreboard: no soreness doesn't mean no progress.

cards.q: What matters most when starting strength exercises?
cards.explain: Form first, always. Master the movement light, then add load — that's how strength is built safely.

flashcards.back: 5 minutes of easy movement before harder exercise to prepare muscles and joints.
Increase weekly training volume by no more than ~10% to avoid injury and burnout.
A day off hard training — muscles rebuild during rest, not during workouts.
Delayed-onset muscle soreness (1–2 days after new exercise) — normal, and not a measure of workout quality.

choices: To raise body temperature and prep joints
questions.explain: Five easy minutes makes muscles and joints ready — most beginner strains happen cold.
Cap weekly increases around 10%. Jumping from 20 to 40 minutes invites injury and burnout.
Training is the signal; recovery is the construction. Skip rest and you skip the gains.

questions.q: No soreness after a workout means…
questions.explain: Soreness tracks novelty, not quality. A good familiar workout often leaves no soreness at all.

questions.q: Best way to check your form?
questions.explain: Video doesn't lie. A quick side-angle clip reveals what mirrors and feelings miss.

cards.title: Protein: the repair crew
cards.body: Muscles rebuild with protein — include some at each meal: beans, lentils, eggs, dairy, fish, or meat. You don't need powders; regular food covers beginners completely.

cards.title: Sleep is when you get fitter
cards.body: Deep sleep is when the body releases the most growth hormone and consolidates motor learning. Seven to nine hours beats any supplement. Train hard, sleep harder.
Habit stacking: attach workouts to habits you already have. 'After my morning tea, I do 10 squats.' The existing habit becomes the trigger, so willpower isn't invited to the negotiation.

Make the default easy: shoes by the door, a 15-minute session option, workout clothes laid out. Motivation is weather — unreliable. Environment is climate. Also note: this is general wellness info, not medical advice; check with a professional if you have health conditions.

cards.q: Why is sleep part of a fitness plan?
choices: Recovery hormones peak during deep sleep
cards.explain: Growth hormone peaks in deep sleep and the brain consolidates new movement patterns overnight.

flashcards.back: Supplies the building blocks muscles use to repair and grow after training.
Attaching a new habit to an existing one so the old habit triggers the new behavior.
Non-exercise activity thermogenesis — calories burned by daily movement like walking and fidgeting.
Sleep, rest days, and nutrition working together to turn training stress into adaptation.

choices: Muscles need it to repair and grow
questions.explain: Training breaks muscle down; protein supplies the rebuild. Regular meals cover it for beginners.
'After tea, 10 squats' — the old habit triggers the new one, no willpower required.

questions.q: Best sleep target for active people?
questions.explain: Seven to nine hours is where recovery hormones and motor learning do their best work.
Motivation fluctuates daily; an easy setup (shoes by the door, short sessions) works regardless of mood.
Beans, eggs, dairy, meat — normal meals supply plenty of protein for beginner training.
